sources.citation: Obeng, Patience. 2021. Some phonological processes in Ahanta. Himalayan Journal of Education and Literature 2(2): 1-11. DOI 10.47310/hjel.2021.v02i02.003
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Silent on stress/accent/prominence (a full-text search for stress/accent the full 11-page text: zero hits for stress, accent, pitch, prominence, intonation). Calls Ahanta 'a tone language' (p. 3), says varieties differ in 'sound, tone and lexical items' (p. 2), tense 'marked by tone' (p. 10); every cited form carries H/L tone marks; keyword 'Suprasegments' but only tone is treated.

sources.citation: Dolphyne, Florence Abena & M. E. Kropp Dakubu. 1988. The Volta-Comoé languages. In M. E. Kropp Dakubu (ed.), The Languages of Ghana, ch. 3, pp. 50-90 approx. London: Kegan Paul International.

sources.note: Family-level survey stating the Tano (incl. Ahanta) languages are two-tone languages with phonemic H/L; PHOIBLE's Ahanta source; would supply a citable tonal statement if no Ahanta-specific one is found.

sources.access_detail: held in print at Harvard (Widener Library, call number 2235.17.50 no. 23); ask your own library for a scan or interlibrary loan (also digitized at HathiTrust, search-only (in copyright))
sources.note: The only dedicated phonology of Ahanta; has a §3.2 Tone (2 phonemic tones H/L, lexical and grammatical) and a 'Suprasegmental phonology' section — the one place a statement on stress would be made. Google Books snippet search finds no 'stress' but is not exhaustive.
